"Ran! Come on back!"

Rina looked back down at the tiny seed in the fresh soil. She had been given strict instructions not to let anyone see it, not even Ran. She had to hope for the former.

    data = sys.stdin.read().strip().split()
    idx = 0

    # Read N

    brackets = []

    # Read M

    books = []
    for _ in range(M):

There are N boards arranged in a line and numbered from 1 to N (left to right). The i-th board is B_i millimetres wide and has strength S_i. When the bookshelf is assembled, every pair of neighbouring boards must overlap by at least one millimetre, so the total width of the finished shelf is
    (sum of all B_i) − (sum of every overlap).
Because the boards preserve their relative left-right order, any choice of overlaps is equivalent to choosing N−1 integer amounts X_1 … X_{N−1}, where  X_i ≥ 1 is the overlap between board i and board i+1, and the total overlapped length is X_1 + … + X_{N−1}.

The shelf is stable only if every board is stronger than the total overlap on its two sides.  For the left-most board the relevant overlap is X_1, for the right-most board it is X_{N−1}, and for every internal board i (2 ≤ i ≤ N−1) it is X_{i−1} + X_i.

Formally, a choice of the X_i is safe if
    S_1 ≥ X_1,
    S_i ≥ X_{i−1} + X_i   for every i = 2 … N−1,
    S_N ≥ X_{N−1}.
The value of the whole shelf is defined as the total overlapped length
    V = X_1 + X_2 + … + X_{N−1}.
Your job is to choose the overlaps so that V is as large as possible while still keeping the shelf stable.

It is guaranteed that the sum of all B_i does not exceed 1 000 000.

Print a single integer – the maximum achievable value of V.

- **Meaning:** Indicates location — the ornament was on the shelf before it was knocked off.

**"Knocked off a ornament from the shelf" = Accidentally hit and made a decorative item fall off the shelf.**

512.completion:
covered it with dirt and gently patted it down. "Okay," I whispered to the tiny seed. "Time to grow."
Tiny blooms
Days passed, and I checked the little spot every day. I watched for any sign that my wildflower seed had started its grand adventure. At first, nothing changed. Then one morning, I saw it—a tiny green sprout poking up through the earth.
I smiled. The first sign of life.
As weeks turned to months, the little plant grew taller and sent out the tiniest green leaves. I was so proud, but I had to wait. Wildflowers don't rush. They take their time, soaking in sun and rain, growing strong roots.
Finally, the day came. A cluster of tiny blooms appeared where I had placed the seed. They weren't the biggest or showiest flowers, but they shone in the sunlight, a splash of purple and yellow among the green. I knelt beside them, my heart full.
A garden lesson
Tending a wildflower seed taught me a lot. It taught me patience. It showed me how a little bit of hope and care can turn into something beautiful. It reminded me that not everything grows fast, but everything grows if you give it a chance.
As I watched the flowers sway in the gentle breeze, I felt grateful—not just for the flowers, but for the quiet lesson they gave me. That sometimes, waiting and believing are the best things we can do for a seed, for a garden, or even for ourselves.
And so, the wildflowers grew, and so did I.
The pollinator sanctuary not only attracted bees and butterflies but also became a source of inspiration for the neighborhood kids. Soon, others began planting their own wildflower patches, and the once vacant lot transformed into a vibrant, blooming oasis.
***
When you plant a seed of hope, you might not know what it will become. But with patience, care, and a little faith, you may just witness a burst of color and life where once there was only earth and dreams.
So next time you find a forgotten spot, maybe plant a wildflower seed. Someday, you may look up and see a world more beautiful than you ever imagined.

As the afternoon heat began to settle over her backyard, Rina swayed in her hammock beneath the old oak tree, trying to imagine what would bloom from the seed she'd planted earlier. Her mind wandered through the possibilities: it could be a daisy, its petals like little suns; it could be a lily, standing tall and proud; or maybe even a tulip, striped like a jewel. But something deep inside her hoped for the unexpected, the flower that didn't have a name, the kind that came from dreams rather than from gardens she'd seen before.
Hours passed. Fireflies began their evening dance, and the sky turned a gentle lavender. Rina slipped out of her hammock, her feet soundless on the warm grass, and strode towards the flowerbed. The stars were coming out, and she could just make out the little lump where the seed was planted.
She knelt, heart fluttering with anticipation. Gently, she reached out and brushed away the dark earth around the planted seed. Nothing had changed—except for a tiny green shoot, no bigger than a pencil tip, spiraling delicately upwards. Rina's eyes widened. It wasn't a daisy, a lily, or a tulip. It was something she had never seen before, with leaves shaped like little hearts and a stem that shimmered softly in the moonlight.
The flower that finally bloomed was a mix of colors Rina had only dreamt of: petals that shifted from indigo to silver, with hints of turquoise along the edges. It exhaled a sweet scent that made her feel calm and hopeful all at once. Rina realized this flower had grown from a seed of possibility—a reminder that the most beautiful things can come from the unknown.
From that day, Rina learned to cherish the gifts she couldn't have predicted. And whenever she passed by that mysterious flower, she was reminded that sometimes, the loveliest surprises are the ones you let your imagination grow.
